events.title: Adolf von Baeyer begins his indigo research
events.place: Gewerbe-Akademie (Trade Academy), Klosterstraße, Berlin, Prussia
events.summary: Adolf von Baeyer, a lecturer in organic chemistry at Berlin's Gewerbe-Akademie since 1860, began working on indigo in 1865. The work led to his identification of indole and to a partial synthesis of indigotin; in 1870, with A. Emmerling, he reduced isatin to indigo. It was the first step in a 15-year academic–industrial effort to make the dye from coal-tar chemicals.
events.significance: Marks the start of the scientific programme that would end India's natural-indigo economy.

events.title: Baeyer's laboratory syntheses of indigo
events.place: Chemical Laboratory, University of Munich, Bavaria
events.summary: In 1878 Baeyer completed the first laboratory synthesis of indigo (from phenylacetic acid via oxindole and isatin). Between 1880 and 1882 he found two further routes — from cinnamic acid via o-nitrophenylpropiolic acid, and (with Viggo Drewsen) from o-nitrobenzaldehyde and acetone. The 1880 patent was assigned to BASF for 100,000 marks and later extended to Hoechst; BASF sold o-nitrophenylpropiolic acid as 'little indigo' for printing from April 1881, but none of these routes could supply bulk indigo because raw materials such as toluene were scarce (4 t of toluene per tonne of indigo).
events.significance: Proved indigo could be made from coal-tar chemicals, and bound academic chemistry to the German dye firms.

events.title: Heumann's aniline and anthranilic-acid routes; BASF's mercury-catalysed naphthalene oxidation
events.place: Eidgenössisches Polytechnikum (ETH), Zurich, Switzerland
events.summary: In 1890 Zurich professor Karl Heumann published two routes in which phenylglycine (from aniline) or phenylglycine-o-carboxylic acid (from anthranilic acid) is fused with caustic alkali to give indoxyl, which oxidizes in air to indigo; BASF and Hoechst bought the patents. The aniline route gave at most about 10% yield, so BASF pursued the anthranilic-acid route, which needed a cheap way to oxidize naphthalene to phthalic acid. According to BASF's own history, in 1891 a laboratory assistant broke a mercury thermometer during an oleum oxidation and chemist E. Sapper deduced that mercury had catalysed the reaction.
events.significance: Put indigo synthesis on cheap, abundant coal-tar feedstocks (aniline, naphthalene).

events.place: BASF works, Ludwigshafen am Rhein, Germany

events.title: Pfleger's sodamide process; Hoechst becomes the second producer
events.place: Degussa, Gutleutstraße, Frankfurt am Main, Germany
events.summary: Johannes Pfleger of Degussa found that adding sodamide to the alkaline melt made Heumann's cheap aniline-based phenylglycine route give high yields; his US patent 680,395 (13 August 1901) was assigned to Degussa. Hoechst took the patent and set up an 'Indigo Company' with Degussa. It stopped work on an almost finished plant at Gersthofen and converted its Höchst works to the sodamide process for 11 million marks, producing 300 t in 1902 and 800 t in 1903. In the Heumann–Pfleger process, phenylglycine is made from aniline, formaldehyde and hydrogen cyanide (a step BASF adopted in 1925). It remains the standard industrial route today.
events.significance: Created the aniline–sodamide chemistry behind nearly all indigo made since.

events.title: Sodium dithionite ('hydrosulfite') becomes the standard indigo reducing agent
events.place: BASF works, Ludwigshafen am Rhein, Germany
events.summary: In 1906 BASF marketed sodium dithionite (Na2S2O4) as 'Hydrosulfite Conc. BASF'. It is still the dominant reducing agent. Its breakdown products, sulfite and sulfate, are the main chemical load in denim-mill wastewater.

events.title: German synthetic indigo reaches its pre-war peak
events.place: BASF, Ludwigshafen (also Hoechst, Frankfurt-Höchst), Germany
events.summary: BASF made 4,900 t of indigo in 1913 by three parallel processes, its highest output ever; Hoechst made 4,500 t by the sodamide process. Together they exported 10,000 t of synthetic indigo worth 53.3 million marks. In 1897 Germany had imported 12.7 million marks' worth of natural indigo. Prices had fallen from 16 marks/kg at launch to 7 marks/kg in 1904 because of price competition between BASF and Hoechst, then held at about 8 marks/kg under an 'indigo convention'. Refined natural indigo cost 20 marks/kg in 1897.
events.significance: Within 16 years Germany went from indigo importer to near-monopoly exporter.

events.title: India's natural indigo industry collapses
events.place: Tirhut indigo districts (Champaran, Saran, Muzaffarpur, Darbhanga), Bihar, British India
events.summary: Indian indigo exports fell from 187,337 cwt in 1895–96 to 49,252 cwt in 1904–05, and the average export value fell from Rs 285.82 to Rs 169.46 per cwt. Nature reported in 1918 that the area under indigo, nearly 1,700,000 acres in 1895, had shrunk to under 150,000 acres, and that the London price had fallen from 7s–8s per lb in 1897 to 3s in early 1914. By then manufacture had practically ceased everywhere except Bihar. In Bihar's four indigo districts the area fell from 135,769 ha (1894–95) to 9,872 ha (1914–15).
events.significance: The fastest collapse of a major tropical commodity caused by a laboratory substitute.

events.title: War blockade briefly revives Indian indigo; Britain starts its own synthesis
events.place: Champaran district (Motihari), Bihar, British India
events.summary: The Allied naval blockade cut off German exports, and German indigo output fell to zero by 1918. India's indigo area recovered to 300,000 ha by 1916 (Schmidt), or over 750,000 acres in 1916–17 (UF/IFAS), with Madras (344,300 acres) now well ahead of Bihar and Orissa (76,000 acres). Peasant grievances over forced indigo growing in Champaran led to Gandhi's Champaran Satyagraha in 1917. Also in 1917, the Levinstein family made Britain's first synthetic indigo at the seized Hoechst (MLB) works at Ellesmere Port. After the war Swiss, US, Japanese and British firms began producing indigo, and the natural revival ended.
events.significance: The last boom for plantation indigo, and the spread of synthetic capacity beyond Germany.

events.place: Levi Strauss & Co. headquarters, San Francisco, California
events.summary: According to Levi's timeline, US soldiers carried Levi's jeans overseas in the Second World War, which was the product's first international exposure. The company began exporting to Europe in 1959 and set up Levi Strauss International and Levi Strauss Far East in 1965 (Levi Strauss Japan followed in 1971). BASF dates indigo's renaissance to the mid-1960s, 'when blue jeans become a cult item for an entire generation'. BASF made 800–1,600 t of indigo a year from the 1950s to the late 1970s, and at the end of 1967 decided to rebuild its war-damaged plant rather than abandon production.
events.significance: Turned indigo from a declining dye into a global mass-fashion commodity.

events.title: Bacteria engineered to make indigo
events.place: Amgen, Thousand Oaks, California, USA
events.summary: Ensley and colleagues reported in Science (14 Oct 1983) that E. coli carrying naphthalene-oxidation genes from a Pseudomonas putida plasmid (NAH7) turns blue by making indigo from indole. In 1993 an Amgen team (Murdock et al.) built strains that make indigo directly from glucose using at least nine cloned genes. Genencor later refined a glucose fermentation for 'biotech indigo' (Berry et al., 2002). None of these displaced the aniline route. A 2023 review notes that glucose still costs about three times as much as aniline.
events.significance: Start of biological manufacture of indigo as an alternative to petrochemical synthesis.

events.title: Pre-reduced liquid indigo cuts hydrosulfite use
events.place: DyStar indigo plant (former BASF works), Ludwigshafen, Germany
events.summary: DyStar says it introduced the first pre-reduced 'DyStar Indigo Vat 40% Solution' in 1998. A 2023 review dates the first pre-reduced indigo products to 1993. Suppliers reduce indigo by catalytic hydrogenation and ship the leuco-indigo solution under nitrogen, so dye houses need little or no sodium hydrosulfite. DyStar tests cited in the literature found about a ninefold drop in sulphite in dye-house wastewater (27,084 to 3,250 mg/L).

events.title: Berkeley team dyes denim with bacterially made indican
events.place: Department of Bioengineering, University of California, Berkeley
events.summary: Hsu, Dueber and colleagues (Nature Chemical Biology, online 8 January 2018) expressed the indigo plant's glucosyltransferase PtUGT1 (from Polygonum tinctorium) in E. coli to make indican, a stable glucose-protected form of indoxyl. Adding a β-glucosidase at the dyeing step releases indoxyl, which forms indigo inside the cotton fibre. This avoids both the aniline chemistry and the reducing agent. The work was spun out as Huue (formerly Tinctorium), which scaled production to 300 L with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's ABPDU in 2019.

notes.scope: Slice: synthetic revolution and modern era, 1865–present. Eras: bengal 1790–1896, synthetic 1897–1945, denim 1946–1999, revival 2000–present (assigned by event year).
notes.dateConvention: Undated web pages use the access date (2026-09-23) in 'date' and also carry an 'accessed' field. Fiscal-year data use the first calendar year.
notes.keySourceNote: Many 1865–1997 facts come from Helmut Schmidt (1997), who headed BASF indigo production from 1972 to 1992. It is an authoritative but company-affiliated source. Where possible it is cross-checked against NobelPrize.org, primary US patents, Nature (1918) and Kumar (2004).
correctionsToBrief: Levi's patent: US 139,121 (20 May 1873) was issued to Jacob W. Davis of Reno as 'assignor to himself and Levi Strauss & Company'; it is not a joint patent. Google Patents returned HTTP 503, so the USPTO image PDF is cited.

1897 launch: BASF's own chronology page gives no month. The exact date, 10 July 1897, comes from Schmidt 1997; TEXtalks/DyStar say July 1897. '17 years' and '18 million gold marks' are confirmed by BASF (company sources only).

Baeyer's 1878 first synthesis started from phenylacetic acid (via oxindole and isatin); the isatin→indigo step dates from 1870. The 1880 route used cinnamic/o-nitrocinnamic acid, and Baeyer–Drewsen (1882) used o-nitrobenzaldehyde + acetone.
BASF's 'Formula for Success' page says 'In 1800, BASF acquires the patent of Adolf von Baeyer'. That is a typo for 1880.
Schmidt's jeans figure is 500 million pairs a year (end of the 1970s). A pen mark on the scanned PDF makes the OCR read '509'.
Sodium dithionite: BASF introduced 'Hydrosulfite Conc. BASF' in 1906 (Schmidt).
Pre-reduced indigo: DyStar claims the first 40% solution in 1998; Linke et al. 2023 say pre-reduced products date from 1993. No BASF 1990s launch was verified.
Archroma 'Denisol' is real: Denisol Pure Indigo 30 (aniline-free) was launched on 28 May 2018.

Genencor was not the 1983 discoverer as far as can be verified. Ensley et al. 1983 (Science) had no affiliation in PubMed; Murdock et al. 1993 was Amgen; Genencor's work is Berry et al. 2002. The brief's 'Murdock et al. 1993 Science' is actually Bio/Technology 11:381-386.
Levi's LCA: 3,781 L is water consumption for a medium-stonewash 501, published 2015 (study begun 2013). Levi's first LCA was in 2007.
Cone White Oak: opened April 1905 and closed 31 Dec 2017 (confirmed).

The 1913 synthetic share of world supply (~96%) could not be verified from a citable source and is omitted. No year-by-year German export series was found; only 1904 (value), 1913 (volume and value) and the 1897 import value.
Lesotho: the Guardian's 2019 coverage was about sexual coercion in denim factories. The pollution evidence comes from the Sunday Times via CBS (2009) and MNN/LESCIJ (2023).
Isaac Newton is pre-1790 and outside the era scheme. He is recorded under notes.culture, not as an event.
apocryphalOrContested: Broken mercury thermometer (1891, E. Sapper, BASF): documented only in BASF-affiliated retellings; treat as company lore.
Kaihara's 'Japan's first rope-dyeing machine, 1970' is a company claim, disputed by other mills.
'A factory in Inner Mongolia makes >50% of world indigo': seen in a search snippet with no traceable source; dropped.
UNB (Univ. of New Brunswick) lab handout: claims 'current annual production is about 5000 tons' and a '$250 M' Hoechst retrofit. Contradicted by better sources; not used.
dataGaps: No authoritative modern figure for world synthetic indigo output or China's share. Estimates range from 50,000 to 88,000 t (and 96,860 t from market research). C&EN (2023) says only 'most indigo is produced' in China. Leads: China Dyestuff Industry Association statistics; USITC reports 3310/3846 on synthetic indigo from China (usitc.gov blocked automated access, HTTP 403); Ullmann's 'Indigo and Indigo Colorants' (Paul, Blackburn, Bechtold 2021, paywalled).

Main producers named in verified sources: DyStar (Nanjing; owned by Zhejiang Longsheng), Jiangsu Taifeng Chemical / Wonderful Chemical (US anti-dumping order 2000), Archroma (Pakistan), and historically BASF, Hoechst and Buffalo Color (US). Other Chinese names (Liyang Skyblue / Liyang Brother, Wuxin, Chongqing Huacai) appear only in trade notices or market research.

culture.detail: In his 1672 'New Theory about Light and Colors' (Phil.
